title: Indicating Resolver Support of DNSSEC
summary: Proposes using a bit in the EDNS0 header, the DO bit, so a resolver can say it understands DNSSEC records. Servers then add DNSSEC data to responses only when asked. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: The DNSSEC OK bit tells a DNS server that the resolver can accept DNSSEC records. The server can then avoid adding those records to replies for clients that did not ask for them.

questions: how does a resolver signal dnssec support
what is the dnssec ok bit
what does the do bit do in dns
why does dnssec cause tcp fallback
subtitle: A bit in an EDNS0 query tells a DNS server whether the resolver can accept DNSSEC records.

tldr.problem: DNSSEC records can make responses too large for older DNS clients and create extra retries or failures when sent to resolvers that cannot use them.
tldr.mechanism: The resolver sets the DNSSEC OK bit in the EDNS0 OPT record. A DNSSEC-aware server includes DNSSEC security records only when the query asks for them, except for explicit record queries and transfers.
tldr.outcome: The DO bit lets resolvers signal that they can accept DNSSEC records. RFC 3225 has been updated by RFC 4033, RFC 4034 and RFC 4035.

facts.label: Flag position
facts.value: Most significant bit of the EDNS0 Z field

today: RFC 3225 is a Proposed Standard published in December 2001. It has been updated by RFC 4033, RFC 4034 and RFC 4035.

sections.title: Why Resolver Support Must Be Explicit
sections.content:
DNSSEC-aware servers may include SIG, KEY or NXT records when answering for a signed zone. RFC 3225 calls these DNSSEC security records. A resolver that cannot process them should not receive them automatically.

The RFC assumes resolver support is binary: a resolver either accepts all DNSSEC security records or none. It therefore uses one bit to tell the server whether the resolver is prepared to receive them.
sections.plainLanguage: A DNSSEC-aware server needs to know whether a resolver can receive DNSSEC records. One flag bit provides that signal.

sections.title: The Cost of Extra DNS Records
sections.content:
Classic DNS over UDP is limited to 512 bytes. Adding DNSSEC records makes responses more likely to be truncated, after which a resolver may retry using TCP. The RFC says this typically takes five packets for a query and response instead of two.

These retries add delay and traffic, increase the chance of timeouts and load nameservers. The RFC also reports that some early non-DNSSEC-aware resolvers failed or ignored responses containing security records.
sections.plainLanguage: Security records can make an answer too large for a classic UDP response. The resolver may need a longer TCP exchange, which uses more packets and can take longer.

sections.title: Where the DO Bit Is Located
sections.content:
The DNSSEC OK (DO) bit is the most significant bit of the Z field in the EDNS0 OPT record. The RFC places it in the extended RCODE and flags portion of that record, rather than in the classic DNS header where bits are scarce.

The RFC does not treat the presence of EDNS0 by itself as evidence of DNSSEC support. An application may use EDNS0 for other purposes and still be unable to handle DNSSEC security records.
sections.plainLanguage: The DO bit is in the extra EDNS0 record, not the crowded classic DNS header. Using EDNS0 alone does not mean a resolver accepts DNSSEC records.

sections.title: How Resolvers and Servers Use DO
sections.content:
When DO is set to one in a query, the resolver can accept DNSSEC security records. When it is zero, the server MUST NOT return SIG, KEY or NXT records unless they were explicitly queried for. The server copies the query's DO bit into the response.

A recursive DNSSEC-aware server MUST set DO on its own recursive queries. If the client did not set DO, the recursive server removes security records before replying, without changing cached data. If a DO query receives NOTIMP, FORMERR or SERVFAIL, the resolver SHOULD retry without EDNS0.
sections.plainLanguage: With DO set, the resolver asks to receive DNSSEC records. A recursive server can request those records upstream and remove them before replying to a client that did not ask for them.

sections.title: Interpreting Missing Security Records
sections.content:
If a response to a query with DO set contains no DNSSEC records, the resolver MUST NOT assume that the zone has no security information. An attacker may have forged the response or changed the query by clearing its DO bit.

The RFC reserves the leftmost bit of the EDNS0 extended flags as the DNSSEC OK bit. It defines the signaling behavior but does not make the absence of records proof that a zone is unsigned.
sections.plainLanguage: Missing DNSSEC records do not prove that a zone has no security information. A response may have been forged, or the request may have been changed in transit.
